parts.article:
Some views on the use of headphones
 
Whether wearing headphones at work, or in other areas of everyday life, is a good thing or a bad thing has generated a lot of research and opinion
 
(A) To visit a typical modern office today is to walk into a room with possibly a dozen songs playing simultaneously but to hear none of them. Up to half of younger workers listen to music on their headphones, and nearly all of them think it makes them better at their jobs. In survey after survey, people report with confidence that music makes them happier, better at concentrating, and more productive. Scientists do not share this belief; they maintain that listening to music hurts people's ability to recall other things they should be doing, and any pop song, loud or soft, reduces overall performance for both extroverts and introverts. A Taiwanese study linked music that has lyrics to lower marks on concentration tests for college students, and other research has shown music with lyrics scrambles our brains' verbal-processing skills. “As silence has the best overall performance, it would still be advisable that people work in silence,” another reporter dryly concluded. The question is therefore: if headphones are so bad for productivity, why do so many people at work have them? One factor to consider is that countries like the USA have moved from a farming and manufacturing economy to a service economy, with an emphasis on jobs in offices that require higher levels of concentration, reflection and creativity. As an estimated 70 percent of office workers work in open-plan office spaces, it is more important to create one's own enclosing bubble of sound. Lending strength to the argument for headphones at work is evidence that music relaxes our muscles, improves our mood, and may even moderately reduce blood pressure, heart rate and anxiety.
 
(B) The story of headphones began in 1910, when the US Navy received an odd letter written in purple ink on blue-and-pink paper. The letter writer, an eccentric inventor and repairman named Nathaniel Baldwin, from the US state of Utah, made what at the time was an astonishing claim: he had built, in his kitchen, a new kind of headset that could amplify sound. This was an opportune invention for the Navy, which asked for a sound test and then enthusiastically adopted the headsets, later called headphones, and used them in World War I for naval radio communication.
 
(C) The purpose of headphones is to concentrate a quiet and private sound in the ear of the listener, which is a radical departure from music's social purpose in history. “Music, together with dance, co-evolved biologically and culturally to serve as a technology of social bonding,” Nils L. Wallin and Björn Merker wrote in The Origins of Music. Songs don't leave behind bones, but evidence of musical notation dates back to Sumeria, 3,500 years ago, and in 1995 archaeologists discovered a bone flute in southern Europe estimated to be 44,000 years old. If music evolved as a social glue for the species, as a way to make groups and keep them together, headphones have done what writing and literacy did for language – they made music private.
 
(D) Author and columnist Stephen Marche wrote that separation from other people is one of the first things ordinary Americans spend their money achieving. It is “a by-product of a long-standing national appetite for independence,” he said. Americans are not alone in their desire for personal independence and privacy. Marche is right; wealth can buy – and modern technology can deliver – personal independence, and it is this that people have always sought. Dr Michael Bull, an expert on personal music devices from the University of Sussex in the UK, has repeatedly made the larger point that personal music devices change how we relate to public spaces. Controlling our public spaces is more important now that more people are moving from the edges of cities to live in urban centres. “With the urban space, the more it's inhabited, the safer you feel,” Bull says. “You feel safe if you can feel people there, but you don't want to interact with them.” Headphones create shields for wearers, separating them from other people and their surroundings. Headphones have their own rules of good manners; they are like wearing a “Do not disturb” sign. We assume that people wearing them are busy and we should respect their privacy, so now people wear them to appear busy. In fact, it is now becoming quite common for people not to listen to anything at all, but just to wear headphones.
 
(E) However, as pointed out at the beginning of this piece, although scientists have stated that headphones are bad for productivity, people still wear them at work. It is not just that headphones create privacy out of public areas, but also that music causes people to relax and reflect and pause. The outcome of relaxation, reflection and pausing at work won't be captured in minute-to-minute productivity metrics. What must be considered is that in moments of extreme focus, our attention radiates outward, toward the problem, rather than inward, on how to solve the problem. However, with music “When our minds are at ease, we're more likely to direct the spotlight of attention inward,” Jonah Lehrer wrote in his book Imagine: How Creativity Works. “The answers have been there all along. We just weren't listening.” In a crowded world, real estate is the ultimate scarce resource, and a headphone is a small invisible fence around our minds – making space, creating separation, and helping us listen to ourselves.
parts.questions:
Questions 27-31
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 27-31 on your answer sheet, write.

Q27 Young people are easily persuaded by surveys that listening to music is beneficial.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q28 Different studies share the same conclusions about the desirability of working in silence.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q29 Some doctors recommend wearing headphones to lower blood pressure.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q30 Nathaniel Baldwin was a respected government researcher.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q31 The effect of the invention of headphones is comparable to the effect of the invention of writing.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 32-36
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 32-36 on your answer sheet.

Q32 What does the writer suggest about a service economy?

  • A The work is mentally demanding.
  • B It provides employment for younger workers.
  • C It is a small part of a country's economy.
  • D Workers have to live in urban centres.

Q33 When the writer mentions the historical evidence for early music, he is

  • A emphasizing the diversity of musical forms.
  • B expressing his frustration with the limited archaeological evidence uncovered.
  • C lending support to the view that music has been important in human history.
  • D creating a geographical map of the evolution of music.

Q34 What does the writer say about the social effects of listening to music through headphones?

  • A It has caused a reduction in the number of people who listen to music.
  • B It has increased people's participation in music events.
  • C It has reduced the global variation of music styles.
  • D It has changed the traditional role of music in society.

Q35 What does the writer say about personal independence?

  • A Americans are unique in their desire for personal independence.
  • B Personal independence is something that can be purchased.
  • C Striving for personal independence is a recent phenomenon.
  • D Personal independence destroys social connections.

Q36 Why does the writer quote Jonah Lehrer in the last paragraph?

  • A To support the writer's own view.
  • B To draw attention to an authoritative book about music.
  • C To raise awareness of people's loss of listening skills.
  • D To illustrate how music brings people closer to each other.
Questions 37-40
Complete the summary using the list of words, A-I, below.
Dr Michael Bull believes that listening to music through headphones has changed the the wearers of headphones have with public spaces. Living in the centre of cities is becoming popular, as people become less keen on living in the . In densely populated city centres, headphones form that isolate people from fellow citizens and from their environment. Wearers of headphones are treated with that other people do not receive. This is because if we see someone wearing headphones, we believe they must be occupied in some way and should not be interrupted.
  • A courtesy
  • B relationship
  • C difficulty
  • D countryside
  • E suburbs
  • F language
  • G barriers
  • H obstacles
  • I disapproval

reference:
Q27

干扰 不要看到“survey”和“believe”就觉得有因果关系，文中强调的是他们自己的看法，而非被调查改变了看法。

句子 (Paragraph A) "In survey after survey, people report with confidence that music makes them happier, better at concentrating, and more productive."

解析 A段提到年轻人自信地报告（report with confidence）音乐让他们更好，但文中并没有说他们是被调查“说服（persuaded）”的，这属于无中生有，选 NOT GIVEN。

Q28

解析 A段列举了科学家观点、台湾的研究和其他研究，都指向同一个结论：“silence has the best overall performance（安静时表现最好）”，即结论一致，选 YES。

干扰 文中虽然提到了不同的研究来源（Scientists, Taiwanese study, other research），但它们的落脚点都是“music hurts... / lower marks”，即支持安静。

句子 (Paragraph A) "Scientists do not share this belief... A Taiwanese study linked music... to lower marks... 'As silence has the best overall performance, it would still be advisable that people work in silence,' another reporter dryly concluded."

Q29

解析 A段虽然提到证据表明音乐可以“适度降低血压（moderately reduce blood pressure）”，但从未提及有“医生推荐（doctors recommend）”通过戴耳机来做这件事，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 哪怕科学事实是对的（音乐降血压），只要文中没提到“医生推荐”这个动作，就是NG。

句子 (Paragraph A) "...music relaxes our muscles, improves our mood, and may even moderately reduce blood pressure, heart rate and anxiety."

Q30

句子 (Paragraph B) "The letter writer, an eccentric inventor and repairman named Nathaniel Baldwin... made what at the time was an astonishing claim..."

解析 B段明确介绍Baldwin是一位“古怪的发明家和修理工（eccentric inventor and repairman）”，他在厨房里造出了耳机，并非受人尊敬的政府研究员，选 NO。

干扰 政府（US Navy）是后来才采用他的发明的，但这不改变他原本只是个民间“怪人”的身份。

Q31

解析 C段末尾明确对比：耳机对音乐的作用，就像写作和识字对语言的作用一样（did what writing and literacy did for language）——使之私密化，选 YES。

干扰 只要看到文中将两者进行了类比（headphones have done what writing... did），即可判定为Yes。

句子 (Paragraph C) "...headphones have done what writing and literacy did for language – they made music private."

Q32

解析 A段提到服务型经济强调办公室工作，这些工作需要“更高水平的专注、反思和创造力”，即脑力要求高，对应选项 A（工作对脑力要求高）。

干扰 选项C说它是国家经济的一小部分，原文说是从农业/制造转型而来（即变主流了）；D说工人必须住市中心是误读，那是后文关于居住趋势的内容。

句子 (Paragraph A) "...a service economy, with an emphasis on jobs in offices that require higher levels of concentration, reflection and creativity."

Q33

解析 C段引用《音乐起源》和骨笛的例子，是为了支持音乐在历史上起到“社会粘合剂（social glue/bonding）”这一重要作用的观点，对应选项 C。

干扰 作者不是为了强调形式多样（A）或抱怨证据有限（B），而是为了构建“音乐原本是社交性的”这一论点，以便与耳机的“私密性”做对比。

句子 (Paragraph C) "Music... co-evolved... to serve as a technology of social bonding... If music evolved as a social glue for the species..."

Q34

干扰 选项A（减少听音乐人数）文中未提及；重点在于“Public/Social”变成了“Private”。

句子 (Paragraph C) "The purpose of headphones is to concentrate a quiet and private sound... which is a radical departure from music's social purpose in history."

解析 C段指出耳机的目的是将声音私有化，这与历史上音乐作为“social purpose（社交目的）”是“radical departure（彻底背离）”，即改变了传统角色，对应选项 D。

Q35

解析 D段提到Stephen Marche的观点是正确的：财富可以购买——现代技术可以交付——个人独立，对应选项 B（个人独立是可以被购买的东西）。

干扰 选项A错，原文明确说“Americans are not alone in their desire...”（美国人并非唯一）；C错，原文说是“long-standing（长期的）”而非“recent（近期的）”。

句子 (Paragraph D) "Marche is right; wealth can buy – and modern technology can deliver – personal independence..."

Q36

解析 E段作者先提出音乐能让人放松反思，然后引用Lehrer的话说明当心智放松时注意力会向内（inward），从而产生洞察力，以此支持自己关于耳机/音乐益处的观点，对应选项 A。

干扰 引用是为了论证观点，而不是为了推荐书（B）或说明人们丧失听力技能（C）。

句子 (Paragraph E) "However, with music... Jonah Lehrer wrote... 'The answers have been there all along. We just weren't listening.'"

Q37

句子 (Paragraph D) "...personal music devices change how we relate to public spaces."

解析 题目说Dr Bull认为耳机改变了佩戴者与公共空间的____，原文D段说“change how we relate to public spaces”，relate的名词形式即relationship，填 B。

干扰 看到“change how we relate”要能立刻反应出这对应名词“relationship”。

Q38

解析 题目说住在市中心变流行，人们不热衷于住在____，原文D段说人们正从“edges of cities（城市边缘）”搬到市中心，城市边缘即郊区，填 E。

干扰 “Edges of cities”是“suburbs”的典型同义替换，虽然D（countryside）也有可能，但在城市规划语境下，与urban centre相对的通常是suburbs。

句子 (Paragraph D) "...controlling our public spaces is more important now that more people are moving from the edges of cities to live in urban centres."

Q39

解析 题目说耳机形成了____将人隔离，原文D段说“Headphones create shields（盾牌/屏障）”，对应选项 G (barriers)。

干扰 “Shields”在这里起到的作用就是阻挡和隔离，与“barriers”同义。

句子 (Paragraph D) "Headphones create shields for wearers, separating them from other people and their surroundings."

Q40

解析 题目说佩戴者受到了别人没有的____，原文D段说耳机有自己的礼貌规则（rules of good manners），我们会“respect their privacy（尊重隐私）”，这是一种礼遇，对应选项 A。

干扰 原文的“good manners”和“respect”都指向礼貌和尊重，即“courtesy”。

句子 (Paragraph D) "Headphones have their own rules of good manners... We assume that people wearing them are busy and we should respect their privacy..."
